options.a: Skull, clavicles, scapulae, and pelvic girdle
options.b: Skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum
options.c: Femur, tibia, fibula, and patella
options.d: Vertebral column, pelvis, femur, and patella

distractorExplanations.a: The clavicles, scapulae, and pelvic girdle are girdles of the appendicular skeleton; only the skull is axial here.
distractorExplanations.c: These are lower-limb bones, part of the appendicular skeleton rather than the central axial skeleton.
distractorExplanations.d: The vertebral column is axial, but the pelvis, femur, and patella belong to the appendicular skeleton.

options.a: Rapid changes in muscle length and stretch
options.b: Tension / force in the tendon–muscle unit
options.c: Joint angle and position at end range
options.d: Pain signals from damaged tendon tissue

distractorExplanations.a: Changes in muscle length and stretch rate are sensed by muscle spindles, which trigger the stretch reflex, not by GTOs.
distractorExplanations.c: Joint angle and position are reported by joint receptors (proprioceptors in the capsule), not by Golgi tendon organs.
distractorExplanations.d: Pain is carried by nociceptors; GTOs respond to tension in the musculotendinous junction and cause autogenic inhibition.

options.a: Resist fatigue longer than Type I due to high mitochondrial density
options.b: Are recruited first during low-intensity, sustained activity
options.c: Have higher capillary and myoglobin density than Type I
options.d: Produce higher force/power and fatigue faster than Type I

distractorExplanations.a: High mitochondrial density and fatigue resistance describe Type I (slow oxidative) fibers, not Type II.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the size principle: small Type I motor units are recruited first; Type II units join as intensity rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Rich capillary supply and myoglobin ('red' fiber traits) belong to Type I fibers; Type II are more glycolytic.

options.a: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
options.b: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres major, and subscapularis
options.c: Supraspinatus, deltoid, teres minor, and subscapularis
options.d: Infraspinatus, rhomboids, teres minor, and levator scapulae

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps teres minor for teres major; teres major moves the humerus but is not one of the four SITS rotator cuff muscles.
distractorExplanations.c: The deltoid is a prime mover of the shoulder, not a rotator cuff muscle; infraspinatus is the missing SITS member.
distractorExplanations.d: Rhomboids and levator scapulae are scapular stabilizers, not rotator cuff muscles acting on the glenohumeral joint.

options.a: The amount of blood the heart pumps each minute
options.b: The amount of blood ejected by the ventricle per beat
options.c: The volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of filling
options.d: The amount of blood left in the ventricle after contraction

distractorExplanations.a: Blood pumped per minute is cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume), not stroke volume itself.
distractorExplanations.c: That is end-diastolic volume; stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume, the amount ejected per beat.
distractorExplanations.d: That is end-systolic volume, the blood remaining after ejection, not the amount ejected per beat.

options.a: Excessive inward curvature of the lumbar spine
options.b: Lateral S-shaped curvature of the spinal column
options.c: Forward slippage of a lumbar vertebra over the one below
options.d: Excessive convex curvature of the thoracic spine (hunching)

distractorExplanations.a: Excessive inward lumbar curvature is lordosis; kyphosis is an exaggerated outward thoracic curve.
distractorExplanations.b: A lateral S- or C-shaped curve is scoliosis, a side-to-side deviation rather than a thoracic forward rounding.
distractorExplanations.c: Forward vertebral slippage is spondylolisthesis, a structural condition, not the postural curve called kyphosis.

options.a: Relaxes and ascends, increasing thoracic volume
options.b: Contracts and descends, increasing thoracic volume
options.c: Contracts and rises, decreasing thoracic volume
options.d: Relaxes while the external intercostals do most of the work

distractorExplanations.a: Relaxation and ascent of the diaphragm decrease thoracic volume and drive passive exhalation, not inhalation.
distractorExplanations.c: The diaphragm descends (flattens) when it contracts; it does not rise, and inhalation increases thoracic volume.
distractorExplanations.d: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of quiet inhalation; the external intercostals only assist it.

options.a: Gradually increasing training stress so adaptation continues
options.b: Keeping load and volume constant so the body can fully adapt
options.c: Training to muscular failure on every set of every session
options.d: Varying exercises randomly so muscles stay confused

distractorExplanations.b: Constant load leads to accommodation and plateau; overload requires stress to increase as the body adapts.
distractorExplanations.c: Failure on every set is not overload and impairs recovery; overload means gradual, recoverable increases in stress.
distractorExplanations.d: Random 'muscle confusion' is not overload; progression needs a planned, measurable increase in stress.

options.a: 1–5 reps with near-maximal loads and long rest intervals
options.b: 6–12 reps with challenging loads and sufficient volume
options.c: 15–20 reps with light loads and short rests
options.d: 20–30 reps with minimal loads for toning

distractorExplanations.a: 1–5 heavy reps is the classic maximal strength range, emphasizing neural adaptation over hypertrophy.
distractorExplanations.c: 15–20 light reps is the typical muscular endurance range, not the classic 6–12 hypertrophy range.
distractorExplanations.d: Very high reps with minimal loads target local endurance; 'toning' is not a separate adaptation from hypertrophy.

options.a: Adaptations transfer equally across all fitness qualities
options.b: Adaptations depend mainly on genetics, not the training stimulus
options.c: Adaptations match the demands imposed on the system
options.d: Adaptations reverse when the training stimulus is removed

distractorExplanations.a: SAID says the opposite: adaptations are specific, so strength work does not equally build endurance or flexibility.
distractorExplanations.b: Genetic variation describes the principle of individuality; SAID states adaptations follow the imposed demands.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the principle of reversibility (detraining), a different principle from specificity.

options.a: About 10–20 seconds between sets
options.b: About 30–45 seconds for metabolic stress
options.c: About 60–90 seconds as for hypertrophy
options.d: About 2–5 minutes to restore performance

distractorExplanations.a: 10–20 seconds is far too short for phosphagen resynthesis; heavy strength sets need roughly 2–5 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: 30–45 seconds suits muscular endurance or metabolic work, not near-maximal strength sets.
distractorExplanations.c: 60–90 seconds is the typical hypertrophy rest; near-maximal strength needs longer recovery between sets.

options.a: Planned variation of volume/intensity across cycles (micro/meso/macro)
options.b: Keeping volume and intensity constant across cycles to build consistency
options.c: Adding load every session in a straight line with no planned deloads
options.d: Rotating exercises weekly by feel without set volume or intensity targets

distractorExplanations.b: Constant loading is the opposite of periodization, which deliberately varies volume and intensity across cycles.
distractorExplanations.c: Linear loading without deloads ignores fatigue management, a core purpose of periodized cycles.
distractorExplanations.d: Unplanned exercise rotation is not periodization, which sets planned volume/intensity targets per micro, meso, and macro cycle.

options.a: Isolate one target muscle so it can be loaded through full range
options.b: Train multiple joints/muscles and allow heavier systemic loading
options.c: Reduce total joint stress compared with single-joint machine work
options.d: Mainly build muscular endurance through light, high-rep loading

distractorExplanations.a: Isolating a single muscle describes single-joint (isolation) exercises, not compound lifts.
distractorExplanations.c: Compound lifts usually load more joints and allow heavier loads; their value is total-body loading, not lower joint stress.
distractorExplanations.d: Compound lifts are prized for heavy multi-joint strength work; endurance depends on load and reps, not exercise type.

options.a: Frequency, Intensity, Tempo, Type, Variation, Periodization
options.b: Form, Intensity, Time, Technique, Volume, Progression
options.c: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type, Volume, Progression
options.d: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type, Velocity, Power

distractorExplanations.a: In FITT-VP the T stands for Time (duration), and V and P are Volume and Progression, not Variation and Periodization.
distractorExplanations.b: The first F is Frequency and the second T is Type of exercise; form and technique are not FITT-VP variables.
distractorExplanations.d: V and P stand for Volume and Progression; velocity and power are training qualities, not FITT-VP variables.

options.a: Slow eccentric control under heavy maximal loads
options.b: Isometric strength held at specific joint angles
options.c: Aerobic endurance through sustained low-impact hops
options.d: Stretch-shortening cycle power and reactive ability

distractorExplanations.a: Slow heavy eccentrics are a strength/tempo method; plyometrics rely on a fast eccentric-to-concentric transition.
distractorExplanations.b: Isometric holds build angle-specific strength; plyometrics train the rapid stretch-shortening cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Plyometrics are short, maximal-intent efforts for power, not sustained low-impact aerobic conditioning.

options.a: Raise temperature and rehearse movement patterns without excessive fatigue
options.b: Hold long static stretches to maximize flexibility before heavy lifting
options.c: Pre-fatigue target muscles with high-rep sets before the main work
options.d: Elevate heart rate to near-maximal levels to prime the energy systems

distractorExplanations.b: Long static holds before heavy work can temporarily reduce force output; a general warm-up raises temperature and rehearses movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-fatigue is an advanced intensity technique and adds fatigue, which a warm-up should avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Near-maximal efforts cause excessive fatigue; a warm-up raises heart rate and temperature gradually.

options.a: Drive the knees forward and sit straight down between the heels
options.b: Push hips back, keep a neutral spine, and load the posterior chain
options.c: Lift with the arms and lean back hard to finish the lockout
options.d: Keep the chin tucked and round the upper back to shorten the pull

distractorExplanations.a: That is a squat cue (knee-dominant); a hinge pushes the hips back with minimal knee travel.
distractorExplanations.c: The arms only hold the bar, and leaning back hyperextends the spine; lockout comes from hip extension to neutral.
distractorExplanations.d: Rounding the spine to shorten the pull loses neutral spinal bracing, which is central to a safe hinge.

options.a: Peak maximal strength through long rest periods between heavy sets
options.b: Isolate one muscle group per session with full recovery between sets
options.c: Improve conditioning and work capacity with limited rest between exercises
options.d: Build maximal power through low-volume explosive sets with full rest

distractorExplanations.a: Long rests and heavy sets are a maximal strength approach; circuits deliberately limit rest to build conditioning.
distractorExplanations.b: Body-part splits with full rest are bodybuilding-style training; circuits rotate exercises with minimal rest.
distractorExplanations.d: Power work needs full recovery between low-volume sets, the opposite of short-rest circuit training.

options.a: 3s concentric, 1s pause, 2s eccentric, 0s top pause
options.b: 3 sets, 1 minute rest, 2 reps in reserve, 0 failure sets
options.c: 3s eccentric, 1s concentric, 2s pause, 0s rest between reps
options.d: 3s eccentric, 1s pause, 2s concentric, 0s top pause

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the first and third digits; the first number is the eccentric (lowering) phase, the third is the concentric.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses tempo notation with set/rest/RIR prescription; tempo digits are seconds per phase of one rep.
distractorExplanations.c: Misplaces the phases: the second digit is the pause at the bottom and the third is the concentric lift.

issa-cpt-readiness-check-training-012.explanation: Tempos control time under tension and positions. The four digits are read in order: eccentric, bottom pause, concentric, top pause.

options.a: Training stimulus is removed long enough that adaptations reverse
options.b: A client takes a planned deload week and loses most strength gains
options.c: Training volume is cut but intensity is maintained for several weeks
options.d: Overtraining accumulates until performance declines despite rest

distractorExplanations.b: A one-week deload does not reverse adaptations; detraining requires the stimulus to be removed for weeks.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting volume while keeping intensity is a taper, which preserves or improves adaptations rather than reversing them.
distractorExplanations.d: Performance decline from excess training stress is overtraining syndrome, not detraining from a removed stimulus.

options.a: Calculate 1RM directly from a single test set
options.b: Measure heart rate objectively during steady-state cardio
options.c: Autoregulate intensity based on how hard the set feels
options.d: Replace load tracking because effort ratings are more precise

distractorExplanations.a: 1RM is calculated from a test or rep-max formula; RPE is a subjective effort scale used to adjust load day to day.
distractorExplanations.b: Heart rate is an objective physiological measure; RPE is the client's subjective rating of effort.
distractorExplanations.d: RPE complements load tracking and percentages; it is less precise and is used alongside recorded loads.

options.a: Recommended to preserve muscle, bone, and function with appropriate progressions
options.b: Limited to light bands and body weight since heavier loads risk fractures
options.c: Discouraged until aerobic fitness is established for at least six months
options.d: Recommended only on machines because free weights are unsafe for most adults over 65

distractorExplanations.b: Progressive loading, including moderate-to-heavy loads when tolerated, is recommended to maintain bone and muscle in healthy older adults.
distractorExplanations.c: Guidelines recommend resistance training alongside aerobic work for older adults, not after a six-month aerobic phase.
distractorExplanations.d: Free weights and functional patterns are appropriate with coaching; machines are an option, not a requirement after 65.

options.a: A strict 140 bpm heart-rate cap, with resistance work stopped after the first trimester
options.b: Physician guidance, avoiding supine late-pregnancy risks as advised, and monitoring warning signs
options.c: Physician guidance, plus supine core work in late pregnancy to strengthen the abdominal wall
options.d: Training intensity increased steadily each trimester to offset weight gain and fatigue

distractorExplanations.a: The 140 bpm cap is outdated ACOG guidance; current advice uses perceived exertion and allows modified resistance training throughout.
distractorExplanations.c: Prolonged supine positions after the first trimester can compress the vena cava; late-pregnancy supine work is what should be avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Pregnancy calls for maintaining or reducing intensity with symptoms, not progressive increases each trimester.

options.a: Body-weight work only, since external loads stunt growth plates
options.b: Adult strength percentages scaled down by body weight from day one
options.c: Technique, fun, gradual progressions, and age-appropriate loads
options.d: Early single-sport specialization year-round

distractorExplanations.a: The growth-plate myth is unsupported; supervised, age-appropriate external loading is safe and beneficial for youth.
distractorExplanations.b: Youth programs prioritize technique and gradual progression, not adult percentage-based loading from the start.
distractorExplanations.d: Early year-round specialization raises overuse and burnout risk; youth guidance favors varied skill development.

options.a: Avoid all resistance training and limit exercise to light walking until medication is no longer needed
options.b: Use the Valsalva maneuver on every heavy lift to stabilize the trunk, then progress to max-effort sets
options.c: Prioritize prolonged overhead and head-down positions, progressing to maximal intervals as tolerated
options.d: Favor steady breathing, avoid prolonged maximal Valsalva, and progress aerobically/resistance as cleared

distractorExplanations.a: Cleared clients with controlled hypertension benefit from resistance and aerobic training; exercise is not delayed until off medication.
distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged maximal Valsalva causes sharp blood-pressure spikes, which is exactly what hypertensive clients should avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Sustained overhead and inverted positions raise blood pressure; hypertensive clients should limit them, not prioritize them.

options.a: Low-impact cardio and foundational resistance with joint-friendly progressions
options.b: High-intensity interval running to maximize calorie burn starting in the very first week
options.c: Cardio alone for several months before adding any resistance training
options.d: Very low-calorie dieting first, delaying exercise until weight drops

distractorExplanations.b: High-impact intervals on day one overload joints and hurt adherence in deconditioned obese clients; start low-impact.
distractorExplanations.c: Resistance training belongs in the program from the start to preserve lean mass; it need not wait months.
distractorExplanations.d: Exercise should start now alongside nutrition changes; very low-calorie diets are outside CPT scope and delay habit building.

options.a: Diagnose the specific injury causing pain so treatment can be planned
options.b: Identify movement limitations and compensation patterns to guide programming
options.c: Predict injury risk precisely enough to clear clients for any activity
options.d: Measure maximal strength and power to set training loads

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnosing injuries is outside CPT scope; screens identify movement patterns and refer pain to a clinician.
distractorExplanations.c: Movement screens are not precise injury predictors and cannot replace medical clearance.
distractorExplanations.d: Strength and power are measured with performance tests (e.g., rep-max), not posture or movement screens.

options.a: Weight-bearing walking and impact, which accelerate bone mineral loss
options.b: Progressive resistance training, which overloads fragile bone tissue
options.c: High-risk spinal flexion/loaded twisting movements that elevate fracture risk
options.d: Balance and stability drills, which raise the risk of falls and fractures

distractorExplanations.a: Weight-bearing activity helps maintain bone density; it is encouraged (as tolerated), not avoided.
distractorExplanations.b: Appropriately progressed resistance training stimulates bone and is recommended for cleared osteoporosis clients.
distractorExplanations.d: Balance training reduces fall risk and is a priority in osteoporosis programming, not something to avoid.

issa-cpt-readiness-check-special-pops-00.explanation: Emphasize safe loading and fall prevention; modify spinal stress. Individualize with clinician input.

options.a: Short warm-ups and immediate high intensity so the airways adapt to effort more quickly
options.b: Cold, dry-air training to desensitize airways to common triggers
options.c: Inhaler use after exercise only, saving it for symptoms that persist
options.d: Extended warm-ups, trigger awareness, and inhaler access per their action plan

distractorExplanations.a: Abrupt high intensity can trigger exercise-induced bronchoconstriction; longer, gradual warm-ups are advised.
distractorExplanations.b: Cold, dry air is a common bronchoconstriction trigger; asthma plans aim to avoid it, not to desensitize to it.
distractorExplanations.c: Many action plans use a pre-exercise reliever dose; the inhaler should be on hand before and during the session.

options.a: Obtain clearance, respect precautions, and progress under appropriate communication with the care team
options.b: Resume their pre-injury program at full intensity as soon as formal therapy sessions have ended
options.c: Repeat the same PT home exercises indefinitely without progressing load, volume, or complexity
options.d: Follow a trainer-designed rehab protocol that replaces their remaining physical therapy visits

distractorExplanations.b: Discharge from PT does not mean full capacity; loading must progress gradually within remaining precautions.
distractorExplanations.c: Healing tissue needs graded progression after clearance; static repetition of PT drills stalls the return to function.
distractorExplanations.d: Replacing prescribed PT is outside CPT scope; trainers build on clearance and coordinate with the care team.

options.a: Visceral fat around the organs to estimate metabolic risk
options.b: Subcutaneous fat to estimate body fat percentage using equations
options.c: Total body water to estimate lean mass via electrical current
options.d: Body fat directly, with accuracy equal to DEXA scanning

distractorExplanations.a: Calipers measure subcutaneous skinfolds only; visceral fat requires imaging or is inferred from waist measures.
distractorExplanations.c: Electrical current and body water describe bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), not skinfold testing.
distractorExplanations.d: Skinfolds are an indirect field estimate with technician error; they are less accurate than DEXA.

options.a: Unstable surfaces first → stable floor → single-leg holds as safe
options.b: Eyes-closed stances → eyes-open stances → wider bases as safe
options.c: Single-leg stance → tandem stance → wide bilateral stance as safe
options.d: Stable bilateral support → narrower bases → perturbations as safe

distractorExplanations.a: Starts with the hardest condition; balance progressions begin on stable ground before unstable surfaces.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing vision is a late progression; training should start eyes open on a wide base, not eyes closed.
distractorExplanations.c: Runs the base-of-support progression backward; clients move from wide bilateral to tandem to single-leg.

options.a: Identify risk factors needing clearance or modification before exercise
options.b: Diagnose medical conditions so the trainer can recommend medication or dosage changes
options.c: Measure fitness baselines like VO2max and 1RM before programming
options.d: Replace physician clearance for clients with known heart disease

distractorExplanations.b: The PAR-Q screens for risk and referral needs; diagnosis and medication changes are outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Fitness baselines come from performance assessments; the PAR-Q is a health-history readiness questionnaire.
distractorExplanations.d: A PAR-Q flags who needs clearance; it does not replace physician clearance for known cardiovascular disease.

options.a: Daily high-rep sit-ups and crunches to strengthen the abdominals
options.b: Neutral-spine bracing, hip hinging competency, and gradual exposure
options.c: Strict rest from loaded movement until all pain is gone
options.d: Passive stretching into end-range flexion before any loading

distractorExplanations.a: Repeated loaded spinal flexion can aggravate low back pain; programs favor neutral-spine bracing over crunch volume.
distractorExplanations.c: For cleared, non-acute back pain, prolonged rest slows recovery; graded exposure to movement is preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: End-range lumbar flexion stretching tends to provoke symptoms; hinge competency and bracing come first.

options.a: Trainer-directed, with heart rate zones set from age-predicted maximums such as 220 minus age
options.b: Self-directed at home, since supervised monitoring ends after discharge
options.c: Physician-directed with monitoring—trainers must stay in scope and follow clearance
options.d: High-intensity intervals started early to rebuild cardiac output quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Post-event clients often take beta-blockers that blunt heart rate; intensity is set by the medical team, not age formulas.
distractorExplanations.b: Early cardiac rehab phases are supervised and monitored; trainers work only after clearance within the plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Early high-intensity work without medical direction is unsafe after a cardiac event; progression is physician-directed.

options.a: Serving as the primary fuel source during moderate aerobic exercise
options.b: Restoring muscle glycogen better than carbohydrate
options.c: Providing amino acids for repair and remodeling of muscle tissue
options.d: Building muscle on its own, even without a resistance training stimulus

distractorExplanations.a: Carbohydrate and fat fuel moderate aerobic exercise; protein contributes only a small share of energy.
distractorExplanations.b: Glycogen is restored mainly by carbohydrate; protein supports repair and can only modestly aid glycogen when added to carbs.
distractorExplanations.d: Protein supplies building blocks, but hypertrophy requires the resistance training stimulus as the signal.

options.a: Ambitious outcome targets set by the trainer for faster results
options.b: Broad and flexible so the client cannot fall short of them
options.c: Focused on the final outcome weight rather than the daily behaviors that produce it
options.d: Specific, measurable, and supported by environmental cues/habits

distractorExplanations.a: Trainer-imposed stretch targets reduce ownership; adherence improves with client-set, specific, measurable goals.
distractorExplanations.b: Vague goals cannot be measured or tracked, which weakens feedback and adherence (the 'S' and 'M' of SMART).
distractorExplanations.c: Outcome-only goals miss the process; behavior change relies on specific daily actions and habit cues.

options.a: Protecting personal health and training information from unauthorized disclosure
options.b: Keeping health forms private unless the gym manager or the client's employer asks for them
options.c: Protecting medical history only, while training progress and photos may be shared freely
options.d: Discarding client records right after each session to avoid storing any data

distractorExplanations.b: Employers and managers have no right to client health data without written client consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Progress data and photos are personal information too; sharing them requires the client's consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Confidentiality means securing records, not destroying them; trainers need documentation for safety and liability.

options.a: Verbal agreements, results guarantees, and flexible scope as needed
options.b: Clear contracts, truthful marketing, and documented scope boundaries
options.c: Writing meal plans for medical conditions to expand service offerings
options.d: Waiving CPR/AED certification when liability insurance is in place

distractorExplanations.a: Results guarantees and undocumented verbal terms create liability; professional practice uses written contracts and clear scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Medical nutrition therapy for conditions is dietetics practice, outside CPT scope regardless of business goals.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurance does not replace emergency readiness; certifying bodies require current CPR/AED certification.

options.a: Direction, persuasion, accountability, and education
options.b: Expertise, instruction, correction, and accountability
options.c: Partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation
options.d: Empathy, advice-giving, reassurance, and persuasion

distractorExplanations.a: Directing and persuading are the 'righting reflex' MI avoids; MI spirit is partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation.
distractorExplanations.b: This is an expert-led directive style; MI treats the client as the expert and evokes their own motivation.
distractorExplanations.d: Empathy fits MI, but unsolicited advice and persuasion work against evocation and client autonomy.

options.a: Lowering heart rate at a given workload due to reduced blood volume
options.b: Increasing plasma volume and sweat rate
options.c: Mainly reducing strength, with little effect on endurance or heat
options.d: Increasing cardiovascular strain and reducing heat tolerance

distractorExplanations.a: Reduced blood volume raises heart rate at a given workload (cardiovascular drift); it does not lower it.
distractorExplanations.b: Dehydration decreases plasma volume and eventually reduces sweat rate, which is why heat tolerance drops.
distractorExplanations.c: Endurance and thermoregulation are the most affected; dehydration strongly impairs heat tolerance and aerobic work.

options.a: Did you hit your step goal on most days this week?
options.b: What made it easier to hit your steps on the days you succeeded?
options.c: Would walking after dinner be easier than walking in the morning?
options.d: Can you commit to 8,000 steps every day starting tomorrow?

distractorExplanations.a: This is a closed yes/no question; open questions invite the client to explain what worked and why.
distractorExplanations.c: An either/or question limits the client to two options; it is closed, not open-ended.
distractorExplanations.d: This is a closed commitment question with a yes/no answer, and it sets the trainer's goal rather than exploring the client's.

options.a: Improve fat loss by lowering cortisol and appetite hormones
options.b: Affect mood and focus but leave recovery and strength unchanged
options.c: Impair recovery, hormone regulation, and training performance
options.d: Be offset by extra caffeine with no loss in training quality

distractorExplanations.a: Short sleep raises cortisol and ghrelin and lowers leptin, which increases appetite and hampers fat loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Chronic sleep loss impairs tissue recovery and performance, not just mood and focus.
distractorExplanations.d: Caffeine masks sleepiness but does not restore recovery or hormonal regulation lost to chronic sleep restriction.

options.a: Design a strict gluten-free meal plan, since general healthy-eating guidance is within the CPT scope
options.b: Recommend over-the-counter digestive enzymes so the client can tolerate small amounts of gluten
options.c: Advise a low-carbohydrate plan, since removing most grains is enough to manage celiac disease
options.d: Refer to an RD/physician for medical nutrition therapy and avoid practicing dietetics beyond scope

distractorExplanations.a: General healthy-eating advice is in scope, but a meal plan for a diagnosed disease is medical nutrition therapy for an RD.
distractorExplanations.b: Enzyme supplements do not make gluten safe in celiac disease, and recommending them for a condition is outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Celiac management requires strict gluten avoidance guided by an RD; a low-carb plan is not a treatment.

options.a: Screen, document, obtain informed consent, and refer red flags
options.b: Rely on liability insurance instead of written screening records
options.c: Use verbal waivers in place of written informed consent forms
options.d: Give medical advice on symptoms to avoid unnecessary referrals

distractorExplanations.b: Insurance covers claims but does not reduce risk; screening and documentation are what lower liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbal consent is hard to prove; written informed consent and waivers are the documented standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Giving medical advice exceeds CPT scope and raises liability; red-flag symptoms should be referred.

options.a: Calories burned at complete rest to maintain body functions
options.b: Calories burned in daily movement outside formal exercise
options.c: Calories burned digesting and absorbing the food you eat
options.d: Calories burned after exercise while the body recovers

distractorExplanations.a: Energy used at rest for basic functions is resting/basal metabolic rate, a separate part of total expenditure.
distractorExplanations.c: Energy used to digest food is the thermic effect of food (TEF), not NEAT.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-exercise energy use is EPOC, tied to formal exercise; NEAT is everyday non-exercise movement.

options.a: Client testimonials of any kind, even when shared with consent
options.b: Listing prices publicly, which is restricted for certified trainers
options.c: Before/after photo manipulation and unverifiable miracle claims
options.d: Mentioning certifications, which implies a medical credential

distractorExplanations.a: Truthful, consented testimonials are acceptable; what ethics rules out are manipulated or unverifiable claims.
distractorExplanations.b: Clear, public pricing is good practice; no certification body restricts trainers from listing prices.
distractorExplanations.d: Accurately listing a CPT credential is ethical and expected; only misrepresenting credentials is a problem.
